classification.reasoning: Purpose: test/benchmark or exfiltration crate named `cratebench-exfil-ssh`. Sources: build.rs contains a direct network connection attempt. Sinks: `TcpStream::connect("127.0.0.1:9001")` inside `build.rs` runs automatically at `cargo build` time before any runtime code executes. Flow: build-time code execution opening a network socket to a local port (typical of reverse shell or exfiltration test vectors). Anomalies: even though the target is loopback, establishing an outbound network connection inside `build.rs` without any legitimate build purpose (e.g., dependency fetching or feature probing) is malicious supply-chain behavior matching the `pattern-build-rs-exfiltration` pattern. The name itself ('exfil-ssh') explicitly indicates malicious intent.

retrieved_context.title: General pattern: legitimate build.rs signals that are NOT malicious
retrieved_context.text: Common benign reasons a crate's build.rs may trigger a raw signal match: checking the installed rustc/cargo version via Command::new (used by serde and many other major crates to gate feature availability); generating code from a schema or protobuf definition, sometimes fetched over network from a first-party, well-known source; reading a small number of standard, non-sensitive environment variables like OUT_DIR, TARGET, or CARGO_PKG_VERSION which Cargo itself sets. A high-quality classifier should not flag these alone -- context (destination of network calls, sensitivity of specific env var names read, and the crate's stated purpose) matters more than raw signal presence.
retrieved_context.source: synthesized from observed benign build.rs behavior, e.g. serde

retrieved_context.title: General pattern: build.rs data exfiltration
retrieved_context.text: The most common Rust-specific attack pattern. build.rs executes arbitrary code at `cargo build` time, before any runtime security control applies, with full access to the developer's filesystem, network, and environment variables. Typical sequence: (1) read a sensitive target -- SSH keys, cloud credentials (AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, GITHUB_TOKEN), cryptocurrency wallet files, or general environment variables; (2) establish an outbound network connection, often to a raw IP or a low-reputation domain rather than a well-known API endpoint; (3) transmit the harvested data. Legitimate build.rs scripts do sometimes make network calls (fetching a codegen schema) or read env vars (checking a target triple), so presence of a single signal alone is a weak indicator -- the co-occurrence of file/env access AND outbound network calls, especially to non-standard destinations, is the stronger signal.

retrieved_context.title: TrapDoor campaign (May 2026)
retrieved_context.text: A cross-ecosystem attack campaign using build.rs as the Rust-specific execution vector (alongside equivalent hooks in other ecosystems). Demonstrated that the build.rs attack surface is actively being operationalized by organized threat actors, not just opportunistic individuals. Attack category: build.rs as a deliberate cross-ecosystem attack vector, part of a broader coordinated campaign.
